title.en: Team and field games: Nadan Panthu Kali, Damru Relay, Aahwan Kabaddi, Chikka-Chikka
Games from every corner of India

text.en: Every region of our country has games of its own. Playing them with kindness makes us better human beings and connects us with our heritage. Today we learn four team games and the exact rules to play them.

Nadan Panthu Kali: form two teams of 7 to 8 students. Mark a field 20 metres wide and 30 metres long with a line in the centre. One team throws the ball into the other team's area using Otta (toss and hit with the same hand), Petta (toss and hit with the other hand) or Pidiyan (toss and hit with the other hand held behind the back).
The other team returns the ball by kicking it beyond the opponent's finish line. If the first team catches the ball they get one point; if the ball is kicked outside the finish line the kicking team gets a point. The first team to score ten points wins. It builds hand-eye and leg-eye coordination.
Damru Relay: two equal teams stand in a straight line facing each other. On the teacher's signal the first runner runs to the opposite line, completes a circle and comes back. As soon as the runner reaches the start, the next student runs. The team whose last student finishes first wins. This builds agility, which is covering distance in different directions in a given time.
Aahwan Kabaddi: two teams face each other 15 to 20 metres apart. Defenders stand with one hand at head level and one at waist level, palms facing. An attacker moves towards them chanting Kabaddi-Kabaddi without taking a breath, claps a defender's palm and sprints back. If defenders tag the attacker before the line, they score 1 point, otherwise the attacker's team does. Everyone takes a turn and the team with most points wins.
Chikka-Chikka: two teams of five students and three houses drawn on the ground. One team stands in a house and the other team surrounds it. Students inside must change houses without being touched by the outside team; if touched they are out. It develops spatial sense and agility. Safety first: ensure no pushing.
After each game, talk in the circle: how would you motivate team members who are losing points, and how do you stay calm when you lose or avoid over-celebrating a win?
Remember the teacher's notes: keep a clear running path, mark the field properly and play gently. Games can be varied - change the field size, ball size, or the number of players.

problem.en: Why does a team in Aahwan Kabaddi score a point when the defenders tag the attacker?

text.en: The attacker must clap a defender's palm and sprint back to their own line.
If the defenders tag the attacker before the line the defenders' team scores 1 point; otherwise the attacker's team does.

why.en: The race back decides the point.

prompt.en: Pick one of these four games and teach its rules to a friend.

requiredIdeas.en: How the game ends and who wins

points.en: Nadan Panthu Kali: first team to ten points wins.
Damru Relay: the team whose last runner finishes first wins.
Aahwan Kabaddi: chant Kabaddi without a breath; points for tag or safe return.
Chikka-Chikka: change houses without being touched.
Play fair, play safely and be kind.
